“Is that everything? That is not much! Many people have offended the Republic and must look out through the little window of the guillotine. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which one is he?”

“I am. I must be, since I am the last.”

Jarvis Lorry has answered all the earlier questions too. He has stepped down and stands with one hand on the carriage door, speaking to a group of officials. They slowly stroll around the coach and climb onto the driver’s seat to inspect the small amount of luggage on the roof. Country people gathered nearby press closer to the doors and stare eagerly inside. A mother holding a small child stretches out its little arm so it can touch the wife of an aristocrat who has gone to the guillotine.

“Here are your papers, Jarvis Lorry, with our signatures added.”

“We may leave, citizen?”

“You may leave. Forward, riders! A pleasant journey!”

“My respects, citizens.—And we are past the first danger!”

Once again these are Jarvis Lorry’s words, as he clasps his hands and looks up. Inside the carriage there is terror, there are tears, and there is the heavy breathing of the unconscious traveller.

“Aren’t we moving too slowly? Can’t they be persuaded to go faster?” asks Lucie, clinging to the old man.

“It would look as though we were escaping, my darling. I must not press them too hard. That would make them suspicious.”

“Look behind us, look behind us! See whether anyone is following!”

“The road is empty, my dearest. So far, nobody is following us.”

We pass clusters of two or three houses, isolated farms, crumbling buildings, dye factories, tanneries, and places like them; then open countryside and rows of bare trees. Beneath us is hard, uneven paving, with soft, deep mud on either side. Sometimes we turn into that bordering mud to escape the stones that rattle and shake us. Sometimes we become stuck in its ruts and boggy patches. Then our impatience becomes so agonising that, in our frantic fear and haste, we want to jump out and run, hide, do anything except remain still.

We leave the open country and pass once more among ruined buildings, lonely farms, dye factories, tanneries, clusters of cottages, and lines of leafless trees. Have these men tricked us, taking another road back? Haven’t we seen this place already? Thank heaven, no. A village. Look behind us, look behind us! Is anyone pursuing us? Quiet—the station for changing horses.

Slowly, our four horses are unharnessed. Slowly, the carriage waits in the little street without horses, looking as if it will never move again. Slowly, fresh horses appear, one at a time. Slowly, the new riders follow, sucking and braiding their whip lashes. Slowly, the old riders count their money, add it up incorrectly, and find the result unsatisfactory.

Biddy wept; to my own eyes the dimming garden, the lane, and the emerging stars had become blurred.

“Was nothing ever found out, Biddy?”

“Nothing.”

“Do you know what has happened to Orlick?”

“Judging by the colour of his clothes, I should say he works in the quarries.”

“Then you must have seen him? Why are you watching that dark tree in the lane?”

“I saw him there the night she died.”

“And that was not the last occasion, Biddy?”

“No. I have seen him there while we have been walking here.—There is no use,” Biddy said, putting a hand on my arm as I moved to rush out. “You know I would never mislead you. He stayed less than a minute, and he has gone.”

To learn that the fellow was still pursuing her revived my fiercest indignation and filled me with bitter hostility toward him. I said so, declaring that I would spare neither money nor trouble to drive him from the district. Little by little she guided me toward calmer conversation, telling me how dearly Joe loved me and how he never complained of anything—she did not say of me; she did not need to, for I understood her meaning—but always fulfilled the duties of his life with a strong hand, a quiet tongue, and a tender heart.

“Indeed, one could scarcely praise him too highly,” I said. “And, Biddy, we must speak of such things often, since naturally I shall be coming down here frequently now. I do not intend to leave poor Joe by himself.”

Biddy did not utter a word.

“Biddy, did you not hear me?”

“Yes, Mr. Pip.”

“Leaving aside your calling me Mr. Pip—which strikes me as rather poor taste, Biddy—what do you mean?”

“What do I mean?” Biddy asked timidly.

“Biddy,” I said with virtuous insistence, “I must ask you to explain what you mean by this.”

“By this?” said Biddy.

“Now, do not repeat my words,” I retorted. “You never used to do that, Biddy.”

“Never used to!” said Biddy. “Oh, Mr. Pip! Used to!”

Well, I thought I might abandon that argument as well. We made another silent circuit of the garden before I returned to my principal position.

“Biddy,” I said, “when I mentioned coming down often to visit Joe, you responded with a very noticeable silence. Be so kind as to tell me why.”

“Are you perfectly certain, then, that you WILL visit him often?” Biddy asked, stopping on the narrow garden path and looking at me beneath the stars with clear, honest eyes.

She left everything behind, keeping only the memory that those things had happened.

Anne had not been back to Kellynch since leaving Lady Russell’s house in September. There had been no need to go, and whenever a visit to the Hall had been possible, she had managed to avoid it. On her first return she took her place again in the Lodge’s elegant, modern rooms, to the great delight of its mistress.

Lady Russell’s happiness at seeing her included some anxiety. She knew who had been visiting Uppercross. Fortunately, Anne seemed to have filled out and grown prettier—or Lady Russell imagined she had. As Anne listened to her compliments, she was amused to connect them with her cousin’s silent admiration. She began to hope that a second spring of youth and beauty might be coming to her.

Once they began talking, Anne soon noticed a change in her own thinking. The matters that had filled her heart when she left Kellynch now seemed less important. She had felt that the Musgroves gave those concerns little attention and had been forced to keep them to herself. Lately she had even stopped thinking about her father, her sister, and Bath. Their affairs had been pushed aside by what was happening at Uppercross. Lady Russell returned to their former hopes and fears, expressing pleasure about the house they had rented in Camden Place and regret that Mrs. Clay remained with them. Anne would have been ashamed to admit how much more she was thinking about Lyme, Louisa Musgrove, and everyone she knew there. The Harvilles’ home and their friendship, along with Captain Benwick’s, interested her far more than her own father’s house in Camden Place or her own sister’s closeness to Mrs. Clay. She actually had to make an effort to seem as concerned as Lady Russell about subjects that naturally ought to have mattered most to her.

Another topic caused a little awkwardness at first. They had to discuss the accident at Lyme. Lady Russell had received a full account of it all within five minutes of arriving the previous day. Nevertheless, they still had to talk about it. She had to ask questions, regret the reckless behaviour, and mourn its consequences. Both women would have to mention Captain Wentworth by name. Anne knew she managed this less easily than Lady Russell. She could not say his name while looking directly into Lady Russell’s eyes until she found a way around her discomfort: she briefly explained what she believed about the attachment between him and Louisa.
